The consequence is in the operators: the + operator has a second meaning, so when either operand is text it joins rather than adds, and a total of 10 read from a field and increased by 5 becomes the text 105, which compares wrongly, sorts wrongly, and cannot be used as a number anywhere else. Multiplication, division, and subtraction have no joining meaning, so they convert silently and give 14 for text 7 times 2, which is why the same value behaves differently with different operators.

answer.exemplar: A debounce keeps a single timer for the whole burst: each call cancels the timer the previous call set and starts a new one, so the work runs once, after the calls have stopped arriving for the length of the wait, and only for the value that arrived last. For a search box that turns three requests into one and stops a service being asked for a prefix the reader has already typed past. The cost is in the wait itself, because no result can begin until the reader has paused, so a long wait feels sluggish and a reader who types once and waits sees nothing at all until it ends. A throttle is the other arrangement: it allows a call at most once per interval, so the first call of a burst goes out at once and later ones wait for the next slot, which keeps the first result fast and pays for it with some requests that will be out of date before they are answered.

answer.exemplar: The build runs on a machine and writes finished files to whatever the site serves, so a value it substitutes is finished before anyone can ask for the file: it is ordinary text in a file the reader downloads, and arriving at it through a build step rather than a hand-written line changes nothing about who can read it. Rotation does not repair the exposure either, because the build that contained the old value keeps being served for as long as readers hold it, and copies are kept by caches, archives, and search engines. A secret therefore belongs on a machine the reader cannot reach: the server reads it from its own configuration, keeps it out of every response body, and makes the call on the page's behalf, so the page receives the answer and never the means of obtaining it. Anything the browser executes, and anything the browser is sent, is readable by the reader by definition.

answer.exemplar: The key is how the runtime matches the page as it is now against the page as it was, so that it can keep the same element, the same focus, the same scroll position, and the same per-item state attached to the same item rather than to the same slot. A position is a property of the list and not of the item, so removing the first of three items renumbers the other two: the runtime sees the item now at position 1 and hands it the state of whatever was at position 1 before, and the item that was last is treated as gone, taking its state with it. A key therefore has to come from the item itself, something that identifies that item across any change to the order, the count, or the contents, which is why an identifier carried by the data is the right source and the position is the wrong one.

questions.explanation: A store is an index, so the first step is finding the entry filed under the very locator the request carries, and a request for a different locator finds nothing and has to go to the origin. The second step is the age of the entry against the lifetime it was stored with, and that comparison is what decides whether the origin needs to be troubled at all: inside the lifetime the entry is used as it stands, outside it the browser has to ask whether anything has changed, and a reply that says nothing has means the stored body is refreshed rather than refetched. Whatever comes back is then filed under the same locator, unless a directive on the response forbids writing it down at all.
